newsitem.title: USA: Wall St. readies new quake bonds for 1997 sale.
newsitem.headline: Wall St. readies new quake bonds for 1997 sale.

text.p: Earthquake risk bonds, which would pay investors reduced returns if a major California earthquake struck during a four-year period, are being readied for sale to institutional investors in early 1997.
The bonds would raise about $1 billion in capital for the new California Earthquake Authority (CEA), which is scheduled to begin selling earthquake insurance policies on December 1.

The planned bond offering is one of a number of similar deals currently being developed by Wall Street to give insurers access to new sources of capital for financial protection in case "the big one" hit.

After Hurricane Andrew in 1992, which generated insured losses of about $15 billion, U.S. insurers have grown increasingly worried about the possibility of a "mega-catastrophe," producing insured losses of up to $100 billion. Such an event would push some insurers to the brink of insolvency and also would overwhelm reinsurers, the industry's traditional financial safety net.

If the earthquake risk bond offering succeeded, it could be one of the first broadly-distributed offerings that would allow an insurer to reduce its catastrophic risk by passing it into the $16 trillion U.S. capital markets, market sources said.
Early feedback on the proposed offering, which is being led by Morgan Stanley and co-managed by Bear Stearns and Goldman Sachs, appears to be generally positive, a Morgan Stanley banker said.

Unlike some of the other attempted catastrophe-linked bond offerings, the earthquake risk bonds would not put an investor's principal at risk, said Jim Tilley, a Morgan Stanley banker leading the deal.
But if a major earthquake struck California in the first four years of the 10-year life of the bond, investors would receive a reduced rate of interest, he said.
"That structure is going to be pretty attractive," Tilley said. "It won't be attractive to everybody; some of them clearly said we're not interested in this."
"But there are many who have said they are interested and they have affirmed that that structure is a very good structure for them, particularly the security of principal."

Investors, however, have said they need to understand more about earthquake risk and they want to see risk-savvy reinsurers participate in the bond offering as a validation of the deal, he said. "Many of the investors, particularly those who could participate in good size, and therefore be among a group of lead investors, have expressed the view that they would like to see some reinsurer participation in the purchase of the bonds," Tilley said.
"Without actively soliciting reinsurers, we've actually had a number who have called us expressing an interest on their part to do that," he said.
Official marketing of the earthquake risk bonds will take place during the two to three months after the Earthquake Authority is up and running, Tilley said.
If the privately-financed, publicly-managed authority launched operations on December 1 as scheduled, the bonds would be priced in early to mid-March, Tilley said.
However, at least 70 percent of the California residential insurance market must agree to participate in the earthquake authority by November 8 for it to become operational.
Although several other insurers have attempted similar catastrophe bond deals in the United States in the past few months, none have succeeded, the sources said.

ACE Ltd earlier this year attempted to raise about $25 to $40 million through a private placement offering of catastrophe-linked bonds that would have put both principal and interest at risk, industry sources said.
But the deal, which was managed by Goldman Sachs, fell through over a disagreement about terms and conditions, sources said.
ACE declined to discuss the details of the deal.
Although the deal did not succeed, an ACE spokeswoman said "we would be very receptive to doing something like this again in the future."
USAA Group also unsuccessfully attempted to sell catastrophe bonds earlier this year to protect it against hurricane losses.
The bonds, which USAA planned to sell to the public through Merrill Lynch, also would have put both principal and interest at risk, industry sources said.
